History:
- Chief complaint: Soreness, cracking and dryness of the skin on the palms with intermittent itching; started ~3–4 months ago after a job change and progressively worsened to the point of missing work for 3 days.
- Onset/duration/progression: Began 3–4 months ago after starting new hotel housekeeping role; progressive, now painful and interfering with work.
- Context/triggers: Frequent exposure to cleaning products (bathrooms) at work; admits she often does not wear gloves.
- Associated symptoms: Intermittent pruritus; occasional bleeding when scratched; generalized mild dry skin on legs. No fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary symptoms; otherwise systemically well.
- Prior treatments tried: E45 emollient (no improvement), oral antihistamine (no improvement).

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
- Medications: Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Family history: Diabetes in family; no known family skin disease.
- Social history: 45-year-old female housekeeper at a hotel; frequent use of cleaning products; not consistently wearing gloves. Non-smoker. Drinks a couple of pints/week.

Physical Examination:
- No clinician-recorded vital signs or formal physical exam in the transcript. (Not recorded.)
- Patient-reported/observed findings:
  - Palmar skin: dry, cracked, sore; intermittent itchiness; bleeding only after scratching.
  - Mild generalized dryness on legs.
- Relevant negatives from history: No fever; no systemic symptoms reported.
- Mental status / general exam: Not recorded.

Impression:
- Primary impression: Probable irritant contact dermatitis (occupational hand dermatitis) — palmar dryness, fissuring and pain beginning after job change with frequent exposure to cleaning agents and inconsistent glove use.
- DDx consistent with transcript (top additional considerations):
  - Allergic contact dermatitis — possible given occupational exposures and pruritus (medium likelihood).
  - Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection) — less likely but possible in chronic palmar dermatitis, especially with diabetes (low–medium likelihood).

Management Plan:
- Immediate advised measures:
  - Avoidance of triggers: strict use of protective gloves when cleaning at all times.
  - Emollients: use stronger emollients routinely, coat hands 3–4 times daily for the next couple of weeks.
  - Topical steroid therapy: prescription provided for a topical steroid cream (agent/dose/route/frequency not documented); prescription to be sent to patient’s pharmacy.
- Other advice:
  - Return for review in ~10–14 days if no improvement; return sooner if lesions worsen, spread, or symptoms escalate.
  - If no response to treatment, consider further evaluation (e.g., fungal testing, patch testing, dermatology referral or alternative therapies) — to be decided at follow-up.
- Patient instructed how to obtain medication: clinician will send prescription to pharmacy.

Patient Summary:
- Laura Parkinson, 45, a hotel housekeeper, developed progressive painful, fissured, itchy palmar dermatitis over 3–4 months after starting a job with frequent cleaning-product exposure and inconsistent glove use. Probable irritant contact dermatitis was diagnosed; she was prescribed a topical steroid, advised intensive emollient use and strict glove use, and told to follow up in 10–14 days or sooner if worse.

Key Takeaways:
- Wear protective gloves at all times when cleaning to avoid further irritation.
- Apply prescribed topical steroid as directed and use emollients 3–4 times daily to restore the skin barrier.
- Return for review in 10–14 days if no improvement or sooner if symptoms worsen/spread.

Next Steps:
- Pharmacy: clinician will send prescription for topical steroid cream (agent/dose not documented).
- Follow-up: outpatient review in ~10–14 days; earlier if worsening.
- If refractory to treatment at follow-up: consider fungal testing, patch testing, and/or dermatology referral.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: clinician-recorded vital signs; formal physical examination findings (lesion descriptions, photos); dermatologic exam (extent/unilateral vs bilateral, borders, scaling vs erythema); medication doses and routes (metformin, prescribed steroid, prior antihistamine, E45 preparation); glycemic control data (e.g., recent HbA1c); any prior skin disease documentation.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted — DDx and clinician impression are consistent.
- Transcript quality: Overall clear conversation with some brief pauses and conversational fillers; no significant inaudible sections.
